new_statements.quote: As is typical in Mon-Khmer languages, well-formed words in Lavïa can be monosyllabic or sesquisyllabic, or a compound comprising elements exemplifying either syllable type. In sesquisyllabic words, a phonologically reduced minor syllable precedes a stressed major syllable. The iambic stress pattern also carries over to compound words, although the first compound element is not phonologically reduced; e.g. kuan ʔiá 'chick'; lai muóʔ 'time'; vu vɨɒ́ʔ 'get dark'; lu lié 'swim around'. [...] Minor syllables are unstressed with indistinctly pronounced vowels.
new_statements.citation: Sun, Jackson T.-S. 2020. Synchronic and diachronic phonology of Lavïa. Language and Linguistics 21(2): 285-330. doi:10.1075/lali.00062.sun
new_statements.locator: p. 287, section 2.1 'Word structure' (second quoted sentence from section 2.2 'The minor syllable', same page)

In sesquisyllabic words, a phonologically reduced minor syl-lable precedes a stressed major syllable. new_statements.rule_in_words: Words are monosyllables, sesquisyllables or compounds of these. Stress falls on the major (last) syllable: in a sesquisyllable the reduced minor syllable (ʔa-, pa-, ka-, ca-, la-, ra-, si-) is unstressed and the following major syllable is stressed; in two-element compounds the second element carries the stress (iambic), even though the first element is a full, unreduced syllable. Effectively fixed word-final stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. Minor-syllable vowels are 'realized with fully articulated vowels in citation or deliberate speech only' (p. 287). The language has no contrastive tone or phonation (pp. 286, 306-307).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (sesquisyllabic words and compound words); citation-form remark concerns minor-syllable vowel realization. Description is of the Banzhe (班哲) village variety, Mengka Town, Ximeng County, from first-hand data collected in Kunming.
new_statements.identity_note: Sun 2020 describes the Lavïa (Masan 马散 / la-vɨɒʔ) variety of Banzhe village, Mengka Town, Ximeng County -- the 'Lavia' component of Glottolog's Lavia-Awalai-Damangnuo Awa (awac1238, ISO vwa). Sun (p. 286, n. 3) argues Lavïa is a distinct Wa-Lawa language and that Awalai and Damangnuo 'may also turn out to be separate languages'; the Xiyun subdialect (Va, tonal, monosyllabic; Sun 2018) is excluded from the awac1238 name and is a different phonological type. The stress statement should be taken as describing Banzhe Lavïa; Sun (n. 24) extends only the absence of tone/register, not the stress remark, to the Masan, Zhongke, Yuesong and Yancheng varieties.

sources.note: p. 287 sec. 2.1 Word structure: words are monosyllabic or sesquisyllabic (or compounds); in sesquisyllables a phonologically reduced minor syllable precedes a stressed major syllable; the iambic pattern carries over to compounds (first element unreduced), e.g. kuan ʔiá 'chick', lai muóʔ 'time'. Sec. 2.2: minor syllables (ʔa-, pa-, ka-, ca-, la-, ra-, si-) are unstressed with indistinct vowels, fully articulated only in citation/deliberate speech. Lavïa is non-tonal, non-phonational (p. 286; concluding remarks pp. 306-307, also for Masan, Zhongke, Yuesong, Yancheng varieties per Zhou et al. 20…

sources.citation: Wikipedia, 'Wa language' (Lavïa section, citing Sun 2018b [= Academia.edu 35782084 preprint of Sun 2020] pp. 286-287, 306)
sources.note: Second-hand paraphrase: 'In disyllables, stress falls at the final syllables (second syllables), preceded by a unstressed minor syllable. This iambic pattern is also found in compound words' -- matches Sun 2020 p. 287, which was then read first-hand. Also lists Awa subdialects Masan (Lavïa), Awalai, Damangnuo, Xiyun (Va) after Zhou, Yan & Chen 2004.

sources.note: Describes standard (Parauk/Aishuai) Wa only; p. 8 (Chapter 1): the Ximeng/Menglian dialects 'referred to in Chinese as Awa... are not represented in this study.' No word-stress rule for Awa; for standard Wa it only notes sesquisyllabic /s./ presyllables (sec. 4.2.1) and an 'emphatic high tone' on the last syllable of an utterance 'or even any stressed word' (Ch. 6).
